text:
Help me write a cover letter. I've taught high school chemistry for 9 years and I'm applying to be a training coordinator at a pharmaceutical manufacturing plant about 30 minutes from me.

About me:
- I teach about 140 students a year across five classes.
- I wrote our school's lab safety program in 2019. Since then we've had no injuries in our labs that needed more than first aid.
- Our AP Chemistry pass rate went from 41% to 58% over the four years I've taught the course.
- Every year I train our new science teachers on lab procedures, about 12 hours each. There have been two a year on average.
- I've never worked in a regulated industry. The job posting asks for experience with GMP training records, which I don't have.
- I use Google Classroom. The plant uses a learning management system I haven't used.

I want the letter to say I can cut their new-hire training time in half. One page.

I'll write the letter once you've answered a few questions. One decision comes first.

**The "cut training time in half" line.** Your record supports "I build training that works and that people follow." Your safety program has gone about seven years with no lab injury beyond first aid. You've taught roughly 1,200 students. Your AP pass rate rose 17 points, which is about 40% more students passing. What your facts don't support is a specific 50% cut. You don't know how long their training takes now, you haven't shortened a training program before, and in a GMP plant much of new-hire training is required content that can't simply be removed.

A hiring manager in pharma will likely read "half" from someone outside the industry as a sign you don't yet understand why their training is as long as it is. That's the opposite of what you need, because your main hurdle is the lack of regulated-industry experience. Nothing in your list answers that objection.

You have two options:
- **Keep the bold claim.** That only works if you have a real basis for it (see question 2).
- **Use a narrower claim you can back up**, for example: "I'd start by finding where your new hires lose time or retain the least, and fix that first." That can include a specific commitment, like a review within a set number of days, but only one you're willing to be held to. Tell me what that is rather than me inventing it.

Which do you want?

**Questions (most important first):**

1. **Do you have any basis for the "half" figure?** For example: you know something about their current onboarding, someone who works there told you it's slow, or you've shortened your own 12-hour teacher training before. If so, the claim may hold up.
2. **Have you done anything about the GMP and records gap?** A course started or finished, or any records you keep now: safety training sign-offs, incident logs, chemical inventory, SDS binders, lab audits. Signed, dated training documentation is close to what GMP records are, and it's the best answer to their main objection.
3. **What happened with the new teachers you trained?** Did they run their labs without incidents? Did any of them say the training helped? About how many have you trained in total?
4. **Why are you leaving teaching, and why this plant?** They'll wonder about both. A one-line answer you're comfortable with will help.
5. **Who is the letter addressed to, and what's the company and exact job title?** Also, does the posting stress anything besides GMP records, like the LMS, SOP writing or audits?
6. **Is there anything else they'll find out anyway?** For example a certification you lack, a start date limited by the school year, or a salary expectation. It's better to address it in the letter than have them find it later.

Answer whichever you can, and I'll leave out anything you don't know rather than guess at it.

1. Not really. I don't know how long their new-hire training takes now. I did rewrite our new-teacher lab training in 2020 and took it from 20 hours to 12. If I can't show I'd cut theirs in half, I'm fine saying what I did at the school instead.

2. I'm enrolled in an online GMP basics course that finishes May 2. I also keep a signed training record for every new teacher I train and for every student's lab safety quiz. The state has audited our lab safety records twice and found nothing.

3. I don't know specifics on how they did afterward, and none of them have given me feedback I could quote. It's been about two a year.

4. I don't have a line for that yet.

5. Karen Doyle, HR manager, Calder Pharmaceuticals, Westfield plant. The title is training coordinator. I don't know if the posting stresses anything else beyond the GMP records and their LMS.

6. I can't start before June 14 because my teaching contract runs until then. For interviews I'm available any weekday after 3:30, or any time during spring break, April 7 to 11.

I dropped the "half" claim and used your 20-to-12-hour rewrite instead. That's a 40% cut you actually made, and it shows the same skill without promising a number for a program you haven't seen.

<final_document>
Dear Ms. Doyle,

I am applying for the Training Coordinator position at Calder Pharmaceuticals' Westfield plant. For nine years I have taught high school chemistry, and much of that work is what this job asks for. I train people to follow procedures where a mistake can hurt someone, and I keep training records that hold up when someone checks them.

In 2019 I wrote my school's lab safety program. Since then about 140 students a year have worked in our labs, and no one has had an injury that needed more than first aid. Every student must pass a lab safety quiz before working in the lab, and I keep a signed record of each one. The state has audited our lab safety records twice and found nothing.

I also train each new science teacher on our lab procedures, about two a year, and keep a signed training record for each of them. In 2020 I rewrote that training and cut it from 20 hours to 12. I don't yet know how your new-hire training is set up, but I would approach it the same way: work out what a new hire needs in order to do the job safely and correctly, teach that well, and cut what doesn't serve it.

My teaching also gets results people can measure. Over the four years I have taught AP Chemistry, our pass rate has risen from 41% to 58%.

I have not worked in a regulated industry, and I have not kept GMP training records. To close that gap, I am taking an online GMP basics course that I will finish on May 2. The setting is new to me, but the habits are ones I already practice: records that are signed, dated, complete and ready for audit. I have not used your learning management system. I currently run all five of my classes through Google Classroom.

My teaching contract runs until June 14, so I could start any time after that date. For interviews I am available any weekday after 3:30 p.m., and at any time during my spring break, April 7 to 11.

Thank you for your time. I would welcome the chance to talk about how I could help train your team at Westfield.

Sincerely,
</final_document>

A few notes:

- **Your name and contact details:** add them under "Sincerely," along with the date at the top.
- **Why you're leaving teaching:** I left this out because you don't have a line for it yet, and I didn't want to put words in your mouth. Ms. Doyle will probably ask in the interview, so it's worth having an answer ready. If you come up with one sentence you're happy with, it could go at the end of the first paragraph.
- **The posting:** I only addressed GMP records and the LMS. If the posting mentions anything else, like writing SOPs or supporting audits, tell me and I'll work it in. Your two clean state audits would fit well there.
